subject: Malahide
claim: William Talbot, youngest son of Richard Talbot of Malahide Castle in Ireland, arrived in Hobart Town in November 1820.
source: Australian Dictionary of Biography: William Talbot

subject: Malahide
claim: Talbot received a location order for 2,000 acres and returned to Van Diemen's Land with six assigned convict servants.
source: Australian Dictionary of Biography: William Talbot

subject: Malahide
claim: After a dispute with George Meredith over land at Great Swan Port, Lieutenant-Governor Arthur reinstated Meredith and gave Talbot 3,000 acres elsewhere; Talbot was allowed a long river frontage at Fingal.
source: Australian Dictionary of Biography: William Talbot
note: The Tasmanian Archives agency note gives the 3,000 acre Fingal grant as 1821; sources differ on the year.

subject: Malahide
claim: Talbot established Malahide between the South Esk and Break O'Day rivers; the adjacent area and town later took the name Fingal.
source: Tintean: A Tale of Two Malahides

subject: Malahide
claim: By 1829 Talbot's flocks numbered about 7,000 sheep and his cattle about 1,000.
source: Australian Dictionary of Biography: William Talbot

subject: Malahide
claim: The original timber homestead burnt down in 1835 and was replaced by the structure that forms the basis of the present house.
source: Tintean: A Tale of Two Malahides

subject: Malahide
claim: William Talbot died unmarried on 22 December 1845; his nephew Samuel Talbot inherited Malahide.
source: Australian Dictionary of Biography: William Talbot

subject: Malahide
claim: Robert Clerk managed Malahide from 1852 to 1880, the longest serving of the nineteenth-century managers.
source: Tintean: A Tale of Two Malahides

subject: Malahide
claim: Richard Gilbert Talbot died intestate in July 1900 and the property was divided between his widow, mother, brother and sister.
source: Tintean: A Tale of Two Malahides

subject: Malahide
claim: Milo Talbot acquired the property in 1938, later restored the homestead and converted a coach house into a gallery for Australian paintings.
source: Tintean: A Tale of Two Malahides

subject: Malahide
claim: Milo Talbot, 7th Baron Talbot de Malahide, died at sea off Piraeus on 14 April 1973; a memorial plaque is in the former St Peter's Anglican Church, Fingal.
source: Monument Australia: Milo John Reginald Talbot

subject: Malahide
claim: After Malahide Castle in Ireland was sold, Rose Talbot made the Tasmanian Malahide her home.
source: Tintean: A Tale of Two Malahides

subject: Malahide
claim: Rose Talbot died at Malahide, Tasmania, in 2009.
source: RTE Documentary on One: Malahide Castle

subject: Malahide
claim: A photograph of the Malahide homestead in 1899 is held by the Tasmanian Archives (PH30/1/3964).
source: Companion to Tasmanian History: Talbot family
note: Archive item

subject: Malahide
claim: The Tasmanian Archives hold records under the agency Malahide Estate (NG2014), described as a homestead and sheep station at Fingal owned by the Talbot family.
note: Archive agency

subject: Sherwood
claim: John and Alice Sherwin arrived on the Brixton and took up land on the River Clyde, naming it Sherwood.

subject: Sherwood
claim: The earlier timber house at Sherwood was burnt in 1830 during a raid by the Big River people in the Black War.
note: Secondary; cites Australian Dictionary of Biography and Connor (1999). Verify against the cited works.

subject: Sherwood
claim: The present Georgian sandstone house and outbuildings (kitchen, bakery, coach house, barn, cottages) were built in 1842 for John Sherwin.
note: Secondary; cites the Australian Heritage Database.

subject: Sherwood
claim: In March 1843 the bushranger Martin Cash and two companions robbed Sherwood, tying up the household and visitors.
note: Secondary; cites the Launceston Examiner (1 April 1843) and Cash's 1870 memoir.

subject: Sherwood irrigation tunnel
claim: Isaac Sherwin directed the hand-cut construction of a 137 m tunnel through sandstone for irrigation, described as one of Tasmania's first irrigation systems.
note: Secondary; cites the Australian Dictionary of Biography. Location at Tunnel Neck is inferred from LIST feature names, not confirmed.

subject: Sherwood
claim: Sherwood was not consistently lived in from the 1950s and was restored in the 1970s by the Sandy Bay Scouts.
note: Secondary; cites the Australian Heritage Database. Year is approximate.

subject: Sherwood
claim: The Tasmanian Heritage Council provisionally entered THR 12036, Sherwood, 1290 Hollow Tree Road, updating the information held for THR 864 (notice dated 22 June 2022).

subject: Sherwood
claim: A 1981 series of colour photographs of the Sherwood homestead and outbuildings is in the Colin Dennison collection, University of Tasmania Special and Rare Collections (AU TAS UTAS ITCCD 2017/14-51).
note: Archive item

subject: Montacute
claim: Captain William Langdon received a 1,500 acre grant in 1823, occupied it in late 1835 and named it after his birthplace, Montacute in Somerset.
note: Secondary; cites the Australian Dictionary of Biography and Australian Heritage Database.

subject: Montacute
claim: John Glover painted Montacute in 1838, one of three homesteads he painted in 1837-38 with Ratho (Bothwell) and Cawood (Ouse).
note: Secondary; cites Hansen (2003).

subject: St James Church
claim: Langdon built St James' Church at Montacute in 1856-57; it was consecrated by Bishop Francis Nixon.
note: Secondary; the page gives the consecration as 11 November 1858 but cites a Courier article dated November 1857.

subject: Montacute
claim: The single-storey slate-roofed sandstone homestead at Montacute is now an abandoned ruin.
note: Secondary; cites the Australian Heritage Database. LIST maps a building classed as Ruin at the heritage point.

subject: Llanberis
claim: Llanberis (formerly Calton Hill) is a two-storey Gothic revival sandstone house built before 1875, with twin gables added around 1890.
note: Secondary; cites the Australian Heritage Database. Year is a latest date.

subject: Strathborough
claim: Strathborough is a two-storey Georgian sandstone house built between 1827 and 1832 with convict labour on land granted to siblings Joseph and Sarah Bradbury, who arrived on the Minerva in 1822.
note: Secondary; cites the Tasmanian Heritage Register.

subject: Strathborough
claim: The Bradburys received 2,000 acres in 1823 and five more acres in 1825 for the house site.
note: Secondary; cites a Central Highlands Council planning application.

subject: Strathborough
claim: The name Strathborough first appears in 1882; the house has since been sold separately from its surrounding land.
note: Secondary; cites the Tasmanian Heritage Register. Matches the cadastre: the house lot and the surrounding land are separate property IDs.

subject: Strathborough
claim: A 2019 restoration of the homestead and stables (published as Hollow Tree House) won the 2020 Tasmanian and national heritage architecture awards.
note: Secondary; cites the Australian Institute of Architects.

subject: Rathmore
claim: Henry Boden Torlesse, a retired Royal Navy lieutenant, received a grant in August 1828 and named it Rathmore; the single-storey sandstone house with attic was built around 1830 with convict labour.
note: Secondary; cites the Australian Heritage Database. The page gives the grant as 2,460 acres in one place and 2,650 in another.

subject: Rathmore
claim: Torlesse mortgaged Rathmore in 1837 and sold it; the estate was later held by one family for over 150 years.
note: Secondary; cites contemporary newspapers.

subject: Rathmore
claim: The early Hollow Tree post office still stands as a cottage on Rathmore.
note: Local history site

subject: Katrine Vale
claim: James Robertson named his 1,000 acre grant Katrine Vale and received 500 more acres in 1824.
note: Secondary; cites the Colonial Secretary Index 1788-1825.
